subsection: 7. Economy and society: world crisis and from free trade to protectionism, 1922–1945

notes.h: Key ideas: free trade, protectionism and semi-state bodies
notes.b: Irish economic policy between 1922 and 1945 swung between two opposite approaches to trade. Four terms describe that swing, and every later block uses them.
points: Free trade means few or no tariffs (taxes on imported goods), so goods cross borders cheaply. It suited an economy that earned its living selling farm produce to Britain, because the Free State wanted Britain's market kept open and its own food and goods cheap.

Protectionism means shielding home industry from foreign competition, using tariffs, quotas (limits on the quantity of a good that may be imported) and licences. Its aims were self-sufficiency, meaning the country supplies its own needs, and jobs for Irish workers.
A semi-state body is a state-owned company run commercially, like a business. Examples are the Electricity Supply Board (ESB), the Irish Sugar Company and Aer Lingus.
Land annuities were the repayments farmers made to the state for the holdings they had bought under the Land Acts, so they were repayments for land purchase, not rent.
The Economic War (1932-38) was the trade war between the Free State and Britain over the annuities, and it hit cattle farmers hardest.

The two main parties were Cumann na nGaedheal, in government from 1922 to 1932 under W.T. Cosgrave, and Fianna Fáil, in government from 1932 under de Valera. Cumann na nGaedheal favoured free trade; Fianna Fáil moved to protection.
notes.tip: Be ready to define free trade and protection in a sentence each, with the policy of each party. Examiners set short questions asking what these terms mean.

notes.h: The Free State's economic inheritance and the impact of partition
notes.b: The Irish Free State came into being on 6 December 1922 with a small, mainly agricultural economy tied to Britain. Partition (1920-22) had separated the industrial North-East from the rest of Ireland, so the new state had less industry to build on.
points: Agriculture was the main employer, and more than 90 per cent of exports, mainly cattle, butter, bacon and eggs, went to Britain. This made the economy very dependent on a single customer.

Partition left the Belfast shipyards (Harland and Wolff), the linen mills and most heavy engineering in Northern Ireland, so the Free State had little industry beyond Dublin brewing (Guinness), biscuits (Jacob's), food processing, and the Ford factory at Cork.

The Free State set up its own customs barrier on the border in April 1923. This interrupted trade in cattle and manufactured goods and created a smuggling economy, because goods taxed on one side were cheaper on the other.

The Currency Act of 1927 created the Saorstát pound at parity with sterling (equal in value), so the Irish pound stayed tied to the British pound and Irish monetary policy, the control of money and interest rates, followed Britain's.

The Free State had a population of under three million, and a small home market limited the scope for industrial growth, because few customers meant a factory could not sell enough to cover its costs.

The civil service, taxation and financial institutions were largely inherited from British rule. The Department of Finance, the ministry that controls government spending, took over the cautious approach of the British Treasury, which affected policy for decades.
notes.tip: A short question may ask what problems the new state faced. Name the dependence on Britain, the loss of industry through partition and the small home market.

notes.h: Cumann na nGaedheal: free trade and agriculture first, 1922-1932
notes.b: The Cumann na nGaedheal governments believed that the farm sector could carry the economy and that low taxes and free trade were the best policy. They aimed at quality exports, low taxes and balanced budgets (spending no more than the state collects).
points: Patrick Hogan, Minister for Agriculture from 1922 to 1932, concentrated on quality exports of beef, butter and bacon to Britain, because a good reputation kept Irish produce selling in its main market.

The Dairy Produce Act and the Creamery Act of 1924 and the Live Stock Breeding Act of 1925 improved standards. The Agricultural Credit Corporation, founded in 1927, lent to farmers, and the government also promoted co-operative creameries.

Ernest Blythe, Minister for Finance from 1923, kept taxes and spending low. His 1924 budget cut the old age pension from 10 shillings to 9 shillings a week, a clear sign of the policy of fiscal conservatism (cautious public finances).
Public-sector pay was also cut, and the government made balanced budgets a priority, so little money was left for new schemes.

A Tariff Commission was set up under the Tariff Commission Act of 1926 to examine applications for protection, but it recommended tariffs on only a limited number of goods, so the government stayed essentially committed to free trade.

The Shannon Scheme, a hydroelectric power station at Ardnacrusha, was approved in 1925 and opened in 1929. It was the chief exception to the policy of low state spending, and it was justified as providing cheap power for industry. The ESB was set up in 1927 to run it.
Critics said that the policy favoured large farmers and left cities, labourers and small farmers with little help, because the state spent so little on anyone outside the export trade.
notes.tip: For a comparison essay, remember that Cumann na nGaedheal stands for stability, farm exports and the Shannon Scheme, but little for the poor. Do not mix up the Tariff Commission of 1926, which led to little protection, with Fianna Fáil's wide tariffs from 1932.

notes.b: McElligott was a civil servant, not a politician, but as Secretary of the Department of Finance he was one of the most influential figures in economic policy for a quarter of a century.
points: James J. McElligott (1893-1974) joined the Department of Finance in 1923, as an Assistant Secretary, and was Secretary of the Department from 1927 to 1953. A Secretary is the senior civil servant, serving whichever party holds power.
He later served as Governor of the Central Bank, from 1953 to 1960.

He worked with Blythe under Cumann na nGaedheal and then with Fianna Fáil's Finance Minister Seán MacEntee in the 1930s, advising ministers on the budget, spending and taxation, and controlling other departments' spending.
His approach was financial orthodoxy: balanced budgets, low taxes, limited state borrowing and strict control of spending by other departments.

He was sceptical of high-spending social programmes and of industrial protection as practised by Seán Lemass, Minister for Industry and Commerce. Finance regularly opposed the cost of new schemes through the 1930s, so he shaped events as well as serving ministers.
Contemporaries in other departments, especially Industry and Commerce, saw Finance as a brake on development.

Historians such as Ronan Fanning, in The Irish Department of Finance 1922-58 (1978), argue that Finance's caution shaped policy for decades and held back growth until the reappraisal of the late 1950s.
notes.tip: For a profile, give his post, the dates (joined 1923, Secretary 1927-53, Central Bank Governor 1953-60), the ministers he advised, his financial orthodoxy and what it meant in practice. Do not confuse him with Blythe, MacEntee or Hogan, who were ministers.

notes.b: The Wall Street Crash and the Depression cut the prices of farm exports and closed foreign markets just as Britain began to move away from free trade. The Free State felt the slump through falling farm prices and closed emigration routes, not through bank failures.
points: The Wall Street Crash of October 1929, the collapse of share prices in the United States, began a worldwide slump, and farm prices fell sharply.
The Free State's farmers lost income because they sold the same produce for less. Emigration to the United States dropped as the American economy shut its doors.
In September 1931 Britain left the gold standard (the system tying a currency to gold), but the Free State kept its currency tied to sterling, so its money moved with Britain's.
Britain moved away from free trade in 1931-32 and turned to protection of its own market, which showed the weakness of Irish dependence on a single market.
Unemployment rose in the towns, and the Cumann na nGaedheal government cut spending and did not bring in tariffs on a large scale, so the policy offered little relief.
The crisis helped Fianna Fáil, which promised protection and self-sufficiency, win the election of February 1932 and take office on 9 March 1932.
Irish farm prices fell steeply in the early 1930s, and the cost of the annuities (the repayments farmers made for their land) became harder to bear.
notes.tip: If asked why Fianna Fáil moved to protection, link the Depression, Britain's change of policy, self-sufficiency, jobs and the 1932 election. Strong answers explain why the Depression made things harder: the dependence on the British market.

notes.b: Fianna Fáil, with Seán Lemass as Minister for Industry and Commerce from 1932, abandoned free trade. Its aims were self-sufficiency and industrial jobs, and it tried to build industry behind tariff walls.
points: Tariffs and quotas were imposed on a wide range of imports, from clothing and shoes to household goods, so that Irish firms could sell to the home market without foreign competition.
The Control of Manufactures Acts of 1932 and 1934 (two Acts) required that majority ownership of manufacturing firms in the Free State be Irish, so that profits and control stayed in the country.
The Industrial Credit Company, set up in 1933, provided capital to new Irish firms.

Semi-state bodies were state-owned companies run commercially. The Irish Sugar Company (1933) ran the beet industry and the sugar factories; the Turf Development Board (1934) and Aer Lingus (1936) were further examples.
Wheat and beet growing were encouraged by subsidy and rose sharply.
By 1939 industrial employment had risen, but many of the new firms were small, inefficient and depended on the home market, so they could not export.
Critics said protection raised prices and did not lead to exports; supporters said it created jobs which free trade would never have provided.
The policy of self-sufficiency was reinforced after 1939 by the Emergency (the Second World War), when imports were cut off.
notes.tip: For the 1930s, give dated policies, not narrative: the Control of Manufactures Acts (1932, 1934), the Industrial Credit Company (1933), Irish Sugar Company (1933), Turf Development Board (1934) and Aer Lingus (1936). The ESB belongs to Cumann na nGaedheal, 1927, not to this list.

notes.h: The Economic War and cattle farmers, 1932-1938
notes.b: The trade war with Britain over the land annuities hit the largest group of farmers hardest. Britain imposed special duties on Irish cattle, beef and butter from July 1932, and the Free State put duties on British goods such as coal and cement.
points: The annuities were about 3 million pounds a year. British duties on cattle, beef and butter from 1932 cut the price of cattle and made many exports uneconomic.
Cattle exports to Britain, the single largest item, fell sharply, and cattle farmers across the country saw their incomes drop, because Britain was their main buyer.
The government paid bounties (payments to exporters) and subsidised wheat and beet to make up for lost income, financed by higher taxes.
The Coal-Cattle Pact of 1935 was a partial truce: Britain took more Irish cattle, and Ireland took British coal.
Dairy farmers and small farmers were affected by the fall in prices, so the cost of the trade war fell on the whole rural economy.

The Anglo-Irish agreement of April 1938 ended the Economic War, settling the annuity dispute for a lump sum of 10 million pounds, but cattle exports did not return to their former level before the war.
notes.tip: If asked why the Economic War hurt cattle farmers, explain that Britain was the main market for cattle and the new duties cut prices and exports. Do not confuse the Pact of 1935, a partial truce, with the agreement of 1938, which ended the dispute.

notes.b: Fianna Fáil spent more than its predecessor on housing and welfare, but resources were limited and poverty remained widespread.
points: The Housing Acts of 1932 and 1936 raised state subsidies, and local authorities built many new houses, helped by slum clearance (pulling down unfit housing) in Dublin.
The Unemployment Assistance Act of 1933 gave relief to those who had run out of insurance benefit.
The Widows' and Orphans' Pensions Act of 1935 introduced a contributory pension scheme, meaning that workers paid in to qualify.
Tenements in Dublin remained overcrowded, and the tuberculosis death rate was high, which shows how much poverty continued despite the new housing.
Emigration fell in the early 1930s as the Depression closed American and British job markets, then rose again in the late 1930s and during the Second World War.
Emigrants' remittances (money sent home) were an important source of income for families in the west, so their reduction in the Depression hurt small farmers.
The marriage bar required women teachers and civil servants to resign on marriage. It was introduced in the 1920s-30s, and it kept married women out of these public posts.
notes.tip: For social policy, name the Housing Acts, Unemployment Assistance (1933) and Widows' and Orphans' Pensions (1935), and add the limit that poverty and emigration continued.

notes.b: Neither free trade nor protection produced rapid growth. Judgements depend on whether the aim is stability, self-sufficiency or living standards.
points: Cumann na nGaedheal's achievement: financial stability, a sound currency, an efficient farm export trade and the Shannon Scheme.
Cumann na nGaedheal's limit: dependence on the British market and low spending left little help for the poor when the Depression came.
Fianna Fáil's achievement: new industries and jobs, a larger state role through semi-state companies and more housing and welfare.
Fianna Fáil's limit: the Economic War, a small and protected market, continued emigration and low living standards.
Why success was hard: a small home market, few natural resources, dependence on Britain, the Depression and then the Second World War.
Contemporary view: supporters of protection held that it was necessary for independence; critics held that it hurt consumers and farmers.

Later view: historians such as Mary Daly (Industrial Development and Irish National Identity, 1922-1939, 1992) and Joe Lee (Ireland 1912-1985, 1989) say that protection created jobs but not an efficient industry, while the Finance Department's caution restricted investment.
notes.tip: In the essay on how effectively governments tackled economic and social problems, state a judgement and compare the two parties. Add that de Valera achieved more in constitutional aims than in economic ones, using the Economic War and the results of protection.

keyTerms.definition: The policy of keeping tariffs low or absent, followed by Cumann na nGaedheal, which suited an economy exporting farm produce to Britain.
The use of tariffs, quotas and licences to shield home industry from imports, adopted by Fianna Fáil from 1932.
The body set up under the Tariff Commission Act 1926 to examine applications for protection.
The government department that controlled the budget and was a centre of financial caution, led by McElligott from 1927 to 1953.
The collapse of the New York stock market in October 1929 that began the world Depression.
The 1932 and 1934 Acts requiring majority Irish ownership of manufacturing firms.
The state-backed lender set up in 1933 to provide capital to new industries.
A company owned by the state but run commercially, such as the ESB, the Irish Sugar Company and Aer Lingus.
The 1932–38 trade dispute with Britain over the land annuities, which hit cattle farmers.
The yearly repayments by farmers who had bought their land under the Land Acts, about £3 million a year.
The rule requiring women in the civil service and national teaching to resign on marriage.
